lessons.title: Swara Shastra: the science of the breath
lessons.body:
स्वर शास्त्र, the science of the {{term:swara|swara}}, is taught mainly in the Shiva Swarodaya, a tantric text written as a dialogue between Shiva and Parvati. Its claim: the breath reveals your state at any moment, and acting in tune with it improves the result. It belongs to the same family as Jyotish — both are about timing an action to the right moment, one by the sky, one by the body.

The three channels

ChannelNostrilLinked toNatureSuited for (per the text)
{{term:ida|Ida}}LeftMoon, coolingReceptive, calm, steadyLasting, gentle, auspicious acts: starting a home, learning, peace talks, travel, buying jewellery, healing
{{term:pingala|Pingala}}RightSun, heatingActive, forcefulHard, quick, competitive acts: debate, physical work, eating, bathing, difficult study, confrontation
{{term:sushumna|Sushumna}}Both equalFire / balanceInward, unstable for worldly workMeditation and prayer only; avoid starting worldly tasks

The rhythm

  • The dominant nostril switches every hour or two through the day.
  • The text ties the day to the lunar fortnight: at sunrise in the bright half (Shukla paksha) the left should flow on the first days; in the dark half (Krishna paksha) the right.
  • Within each nostril’s flow (roughly an hour), the five {{term:tattva|tattvas}} (earth, water, fire, air, ether) are said to rise in turn, read from the breath’s length, direction and feel.

How to check your swara (1 minute)

  1. Sit still, mouth closed.
  2. Close the right nostril with a finger and breathe through the left; then swap.
  3. The side that flows freely is your current swara. If both are equal, it is Sushumna.

What the texts teach beyond timing

  • Self-observation: noticing the breath before acting is itself a pause that improves decisions.
  • Nadi shodhana (alternate-nostril breathing) balances the two channels; a common yoga practice.
  • Health: the text says a swara stuck on one side for a long time signals imbalance.
For you

Use it the way you use Rahu Kaal: a small timing check. Before a negotiation or a hard customer call, a right-nostril (Pingala) flow is the classical match; before writing to someone you care about or planning, the left (Ida). Combine with the Jyotish day picker; do not let it block necessary work.

Modern research confirms a real nasal cycle: the nostrils alternate in congestion, typically every 1–4 hours, regulated by the autonomic nervous system. The Swara claims about outcomes (success, victory, health predictions) have not been tested scientifically. Treat it as a mindfulness and timing practice, not a guarantee. Never force breathing or hold the breath long without a teacher.

Remember
  • Left = Ida = Moon = steady and gentle.
  • Right = Pingala = Sun = forceful and active.
  • Both = Sushumna = meditate, don’t start.
lessons.listen: Swara Shastra is the science of the breath, taught mainly in the Shiva Swarodaya as a dialogue between Shiva and Parvati. It watches which nostril the breath is flowing through. The left nostril is Ida, the lunar channel: cooling, receptive, good for steady, gentle and lasting work. The right is Pingala, the solar channel: heating, active, good for hard, competitive or physical work. When both flow equally, that is Sushumna, said to suit meditation only. The flow switches sides every hour or two. Modern science confirms a real nasal cycle that alternates through the day, but the claims about outcomes have not been tested. Practise by checking your dominant nostril before important actions and simply noticing.

quiz.q: According to Swara Shastra, Sushumna is best for…

o: A real nasal cycle alternates through the day
quiz.w: The nasal cycle is real; the outcome claims are untested.
